0.0.n: This noun names the activity being discussed.

0.1.n: A conversational way to introduce a topic, similar to は.

0.3.n: This gives the length of a study session.

0.4.n: Marks the study time in a shortened expression with the action left unstated.

0.5.n: This gives the number of days spent on the one-hour schedule.

0.6.n: Marks the schedule used as the comparison baseline.

0.7.n: Adds emphasis to より; together they strengthen the comparison.

0.8.n: This gives the length of each shorter study session.

0.9.n: Marks the study time, with the action of studying left unstated.

0.10.n: 間 marks a span of time; here, the shorter sessions are spread across this span.

0.11.n: Links the six-day schedule to 方, the preferred alternative.

0.12.n: In の方が, this identifies the alternative judged more favorably.

0.13.n: Marks the six-day option as what has greater value.

0.14.n: In 意味がある, this refers to usefulness; the speaker leaves out が here.

0.15.n: ある combines with 意味 to describe something as worthwhile.

0.16.n: Short for の, introducing an explanation before です.

0.17.n: Makes the explanation polite as part of んです.

0.18.n: Presents the point as information the speaker wants the listener to recognize.

0.19.n: Invites agreement and softens the assertion.

1.0.n: Together with ので, this politely connects the previous point to its consequence.

1.1.n: In ですので, it introduces a conclusion based on what was just said.

1.2.n: This duration directly describes how long someone studies.

1.3.n: 勉強すれば is the conditional form of 勉強する, presenting studying as a condition.

1.5.n: A personal pronoun commonly used by male speakers.

1.6.n: Links 僕 to the one-month period belonging to the speaker's experience.

1.7.n: Points back to a particular month already mentioned or understood.

1.8.n: This is the speaker's study period used for comparison.

1.9.n: Marks what the five-month period is being compared with using 同じ.

1.10.n: Pairs with と to express equality between the two study periods.

1.11.n: Makes the claimed equivalence approximate rather than exact.

1.12.n: The plain statement ending appears inside the thought reported with と思います.

1.13.n: Marks the preceding statement as the content of the speaker's thought.

1.14.n: The polite form of 思う presents this comparison as the speaker's judgment.

2.0.n: Specifies that the following duration is the combined amount of study time.

2.1.n: Gives the total duration of studying before the next stage.

2.2.n: The past form of 勉強する comes before 後 to mark an action completed beforehand.

2.3.n: Follows 勉強した to locate the next stage later than the studying.

2.4.n: Makes the period after studying the topic of the sentence.

2.6.n: Names the source from which Japanese can be learned.

2.7.n: Marks conversation as the source of learning.

2.9.n: Marks 日本語 as what the learner can pick up.

2.10.n: The ability form of 覚える; here it means picking up language, not merely memorizing isolated facts.

2.11.n: After an ability form, よう helps describe a newly attainable state.

2.12.n: Links よう to なる, marking the state the learner comes to reach.

2.13.n: With 覚えられるように, this describes developing a new ability.

2.14.n: Connects this developing ability to the prediction in the next line.

3.0.n: 後 attaches to the duration to indicate a later point in time.

3.2.n: Marks the approximate future time when the predicted level is reached.

3.3.n: Highlights that future time as the topic; には can suggest by that stage.

3.4.n: Names the language used to form friendships.

3.5.n: Marks Japanese as the means of communication.

3.6.n: With ができる, this describes forming friendships.

3.7.n: Marks 友達 as what comes into being in the expression 友達ができる.

3.8.n: In 友達ができる, できる describes friendships forming, rather than making an object.

3.9.n: The preceding phrase describes what someone can do at this stage of proficiency.

3.10.n: Marks the level reached as the result of change.

3.11.n: With レベルに, なる expresses progressing to a particular proficiency level.

3.12.n: Marks the prediction as the content of 思います.

3.13.n: The polite form of 思う frames the timeline as the speaker's estimate.

0.lit: As for studying, rather than one hour for one day, ten minutes for six days has more value, you know.
0.tip: より marks the comparison baseline, while の方が identifies the option judged better.

1.lit: So, if you study five months, I think it is roughly the same as that one month of mine.
1.tip: すれば is the if-form of する, so 勉強すれば means if you study.

2.lit: After studying six months in total, because you come to be able to learn Japanese from conversation,
2.tip: An ability form followed by ようになる describes gaining an ability you did not previously have.

3.lit: At about ten months later, I think you will reach a level where you can make friends using Japanese.
3.tip: 友達ができる means making friends, with 友達 marked by が rather than を.
